negative.name: connected branching tree is not an extremal path
negative.falseClaim: Every connected simple tree with n edges attains c_n, regardless of its vertex degrees.

hypotheses: X and Y are partitions of the same n-element set
the probability measure is uniform on those n elements
RI = H(X)+H(Y)-H(join)-H(meet), with the maintained refinement order

proofChain.argument: If meet is trivial, the bipartite block graph is connected. One vertex per X/Y block; a nonempty intersection gives one edge of integer weight c, vertex degree a is total incident weight, and total edge weight is n. With phi(t)=t log2(t), H(X)=log2(n)-sum_X phi(a)/n, H(Y) analogously, H(join)=log2(n)-sum_edges phi(c)/n, H(meet)=0. Hence RI=log2(n)-Phi/n with Phi=sum_vertices phi(a)-sum_edges phi(c).

For an edge with weight c>=2, choose one incident block A with size a>=c, pull one atom in that intersection out of A into a new singleton block, and leave the other partition unchanged. The original intersection retains c-1 atoms, so no original graph vertex or connection disappears; the new singleton is a leaf, preserving connectivity and trivial meet. Phi_old-Phi_new=[phi(a)-phi(a-1)]-[phi(c)-phi(c-1)]>=0: phi is strictly convex on positive reals (phi_second(t)=1/(t ln(2))). Thus RI_new>=RI_old, strictly if a>c. The integer potential sum_edges(c-1)=n-edge_count decreases by one; finitely many splits reach discrete join.

When n>=3 and some edge has c>=2, if either endpoint has size greater than c, choose it for a strict improvement. Otherwise both endpoint sizes equal c; connectedness then forces this to be the sole edge and n=c. The first split may preserve Phi. Since n>=3, the remaining edge has weight n-1>=2; split its opposite endpoint, whose size is still n>n-1, to obtain a strict improvement. Therefore any weighted-overlap pair is strictly below the maximum for n>=3.
For integer d>=1, phi(d)>=2(d-1), equality exactly at d=1,2. Equality is direct at 1,2. For real d>=2, the derivative of phi(d)-2(d-1) is log2(d)+1/ln(2)-2>0.

At discrete join every edge weight is one. The connected simple bipartite graph has n edges, v<=n+1 vertices and sum_degrees=2n. Thus Phi=sum phi(d)>=2(2n-v)>=2(n-1), giving RI<=log2(n)-2+2/n=c_n. Equality requires v=n+1 and all degrees in {1,2}: a connected tree with maximum degree two is a path. Conversely a path has two degree-one vertices and n-1 degree-two vertices and attains c_n.

A trivial-meet weighted pair can be split to a simple connected pair without decreasing RI; the latter is bounded by c_n. For n>=3 strict-overlap excludes weighted pairs from equality, leaving exactly simple paths, including their atom relabellings and interchange of X/Y.

For a nontrivial meet, its blocks are the connected components C_t of the block graph, with sizes n_t. X, Y and join refine meet, so entropy chain rules give H(X)=H(meet)+sum_t(n_t/n)H(X|C_t), and likewise for Y and join. Consequently RI=sum_t(n_t/n)RI_t, each restricted pair having trivial meet.

Every RI_t<=c_(n_t). Here c_1=c_2=0; for real x>=2, c_prime(x)=1/(x ln(2))-2/x^2>0. Therefore c_k<c_n for every integer 1<=k<n when n>=3. With more than one component, all n_t<n, and RI<=sum_t(n_t/n)c_(n_t)<c_n. Thus equality for n>=3 forces trivial meet and the path characterization above.

For n=1 the unique partition pair gives RI=0=c_1. For n=2 the two partitions form a chain; for any pair its meet and join are the pair itself in some order, so RI=0=c_2. Hence every pair attains the zero maximum in these two cases.
